prompt:
You are a junior associate at Caldera, Voss & Tanaka, P.C. Supervising partner Alex Carbonneau has assigned you a witness preparation deposition outline for our client, Saltspring Holdings, Inc. The assignment was handed down on May 9, 2026, and Alex wants the first draft on his desk by May 16.

This matter implicates the Ninth Circuit's recent opinion in Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2025), which vacated a district court protective order that had restricted class counsel from using discovery materials in advocacy outside the underlying action. That ruling is central to how this deposition needs to be structured, particularly because Saltspring's exposure likely turns on the permissible scope of discovery material use and how our client's internal policies address that issue.

The outline should identify the witness by role and relationship to Saltspring Holdings and follow standard deposition flow — background and qualifications, foundation, substantive examination topics, and impeachment/closing. For each substantive section, draft open-ended questions aimed at eliciting narrative responses rather than simple yes or no answers. A separate section must address the protective order framework discussed in Stemilt, preparing the witness to testify about Saltspring's internal policies for handling and restricting use of discovery materials obtained in litigation. Foundation-laying questions should be embedded for each likely exhibit or document category. I've attached an excerpt from the witness's prior deposition testimony for your reference — review it for consistency issues and potential impeachment material.

Where the Stemilt opinion's procedural posture is relevant — the class action settlement, the vacatur of the protective order, the limits on counsel's extrinsic use of discovery — anticipate how opposing counsel will likely probe and build cross-examination-style follow-ups into the notes. Flag any areas where you expect attorney-client privilege objections or where the witness needs additional prep, and reference privilege log considerations consistent with Rule 26(b)(5) where appropriate. The outline must account for Rules 26(c) and 30 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

Formatting should follow our standard deposition outline conventions: numbered questions with indented sub-questions under topical headings, Bluebook citations, and a confidential attorney-work-product designation header. Include a cover sheet with placeholders for case caption, witness name, and deposition date, along with preparation notes for Alex's review. The final deliverable should be a clean PDF. Keep in mind that Alex may forward this directly to Saltspring's in-house counsel, so the tone needs to be client-facing and professional throughout.

sections.heading: Introduction
required_content: Context and purpose of the document
paragraphs: This letter serves as a formal demand on behalf of our client, [Worker Name/Group Name], regarding systemic violations of federal and state labor laws and your company’s corresponding legal obligations to provide lawful working conditions, accurate wage compensation, and safe transportation. The purpose of this communication is to outline the clear factual and legal basis for these violations, to demand immediate corrective action, and to provide notice of our client’s intent to pursue all available legal remedies should a resolution not be achieved. This demand is grounded in well-established legal principles governing agricultural employment and is necessitated by your company’s ongoing practices.

Our analysis is guided directly by the binding precedent of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2024). In that decision, the court unequivocally reaffirmed and clarified the obligations of agricultural employers under the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act (AWPA) and related statutes. The court held that employers are liable for ensuring transportation used for workers meets safety standards and that compensation for all hours worked, including mandatory pre- and post-shift activities, must be accurately calculated and paid. *Stemilt* establishes that liability for these statutory violations is not excused by the use of labor contractors or other intermediaries; the agricultural employer bears ultimate responsibility for the working conditions it necessitates.

Your company’s practices, as detailed herein, appear to contravene the very standards upheld in *Stemilt*. Our client has provided information indicating a pattern of practices that fail to ensure safe transportation to and from fields, result in the systematic underpayment of wages for compensable work time, and demonstrate a lack of the necessary recordkeeping mandated by law. These are not isolated incidents but reflect a standard operating procedure that subjects your workers to illegal conditions and economic harm.

Therefore, pursuant to the rights afforded under the AWPA, the Fair Labor Standards Act, and Washington state wage laws, we demand that you immediately cease and remedy all unlawful practices. This includes providing and maintaining safe transportation, paying all owed back wages and damages, implementing lawful recordkeeping systems, and providing your workers with all required disclosures and protections. We require your written response to this demand within thirty (30) days, outlining the specific corrective actions you will undertake. Failure to respond substantively and implement immediate changes will leave our client with no alternative but to initiate formal legal proceedings to enforce the law and seek all appropriate remedies, including statutory damages, back wages, attorneys’ fees, and costs.

sections.heading: Background
required_content: Reference to Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC
paragraphs: The legal standard for determining “employer” status under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) is central to this matter and has been authoritatively clarified by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. In *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2024), the court reaffirmed and applied the “economic realities” test to assess joint employer liability. The court held that an entity may be deemed an employer if it exercises functional control over the workers’ terms and conditions of employment, irrespective of formal contractual designations. This control may be evidenced by the entity’s authority to hire and fire, supervise and control work schedules or conditions of employment, determine the rate and method of payment, and maintain employment records. *Id.* at 1210. The decision underscores that the substance of the working relationship, not its form, governs the inquiry.

Our client, Saltspring Holdings, Inc. (“Saltspring”), is a Washington corporation that operates as a holding company for several affiliated agricultural entities. Saltspring’s corporate structure involves contractual arrangements with third-party labor providers and field managers to cultivate and harvest its produce. While Saltspring maintains ownership of the farmland and ultimate financial interest in the agricultural output, it has traditionally asserted that it does not directly employ the workers on its properties, pointing to staffing agreements that purport to vest employer responsibilities in the labor suppliers.

The analysis in *Columbia Legal Services* is directly applicable to Saltspring’s operational model. A preliminary review indicates that Saltspring, through its agents and supervisors, likely exerts sufficient functional control over the agricultural workers to establish an employment relationship under the FLSA. Evidence suggests Saltspring’s personnel set work schedules, direct daily tasks, provide necessary tools and equipment, and effectively control the worksite where labor is performed. These factors align closely with the indicia of control identified by the Ninth Circuit. Therefore, the legal framework established in *Columbia Legal Services* provides the definitive lens through which Saltspring’s potential liabilities as an employer—including for minimum wage, overtime, and recordkeeping violations—must be analyzed.

sections.heading: Analysis / Argument
paragraphs: The Court's analysis must begin with the threshold question of whether the Defendant's communications to state regulatory agencies constitute protected petitioning activity under the *Noerr-Pennington* doctrine, as codified in this context. The Ninth Circuit's recent and dispositive opinion in *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2025), establishes the governing framework. The court in *Columbia* held that complaints and reports filed with governmental agencies regarding alleged legal violations are "classic" forms of petitioning activity entitled to First Amendment protection. 142 F.4th at 1211. The protection is forfeited only if the petitioning activity is "objectively baseless" and constitutes an attempt to use governmental process itself as an anticompetitive weapon—a showing that requires more than merely losing on the merits of the underlying complaint. *Id.* at 1213-14. The Defendant’s actions in the present matter—filing reports with the Department of Labor and the Office of the Attorney General concerning alleged workplace safety and wage/hour violations—fall squarely within the protected petitioning activity endorsed in *Columbia*. The Plaintiff’s Amended Complaint does not, and cannot, allege facts sufficient to meet the demanding "sham" exception standard. The regulatory agencies’ substantive review and action on the Defendant’s complaints conclusively demonstrates that they were not objectively baseless, thereby immunizing the Defendant from tort liability for those filings.

The Plaintiff’s attempt to characterize the Defendant’s petitions as tortious interference or defamation must fail as a matter of law because such a characterization directly conflicts with the constitutional and statutory protections affirmed in *Columbia*. The Ninth Circuit explicitly rejected the notion that the filing of a petition with the government, even if it results in economic injury to a private party, can form the basis for a tort claim absent the narrow sham exception. 142 F.4th at 1215. To hold otherwise would allow private litigants to use state tort law to chill the fundamental right of petition, subjecting every concerned citizen or competitor who contacts a regulatory agency to potential liability. The law does not permit such an end-run around the First Amendment. The Defendant’s communications were directed at securing governmental action, a purpose at the "core" of the petition right, and any alleged harm to the Plaintiff is incidental to the exercise of that protected right.

Furthermore, the Plaintiff’s allegations concerning statements made outside the formal petitioning process to non-governmental third parties must be analyzed under the established framework for ancillary conduct. *Columbia* instructs that while the petitioning activity itself is protected, a party may be liable for "independent" tortious acts undertaken in conjunction with, but not part of, the petition. 142 F.4th at 1218. The Plaintiff has failed to plead any such independent, actionable tort with the requisite specificity. The alleged statements to other contractors were, as pleaded, merely a recitation of the fact that the Defendant had filed regulatory complaints. Such reporting of one’s own petitioning activity does not constitute an independent tort; it is inextricably intertwined with and ancillary to the protected petition itself. To permit liability here would effectively allow a plaintiff to circumvent petitioning immunity through artful pleading, a result the Ninth Circuit in *Columbia* explicitly foreclosed. Therefore, the Defendant’s motions to dismiss each cause of action are meritorious, as the Complaint in its entirety rests on conduct shielded from civil liability by the precedent of *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: For the foregoing reasons, the Court should grant Plaintiff's Motion for Summary Judgment on the question of liability and deny Defendant's cross-motion. The undisputed material facts, viewed in the light most favorable to no party given their mutual motion practice, conclusively demonstrate that Defendant's policies and practices constitute a pattern or practice of violating the Agricultural Worker Protection Act, 29 U.S.C. § 1801 et seq., and its implementing regulations. Defendant’s willful failure to provide accurate itemized pay statements, maintain required wage records, and furnish employment terms in the manner prescribed by statute is not merely technical noncompliance but a systemic failure that deprives agricultural workers of the basic informational tools necessary to vindicate their rights.

The Ninth Circuit’s reasoning in *Columbia Legal Services v. Stemilt Ag Services, LLC*, 142 F.4th 1201 (9th Cir. 2022), is directly instructive and mandates the relief sought here. As the Court in *Stemilt* recognized, the AWPA’s notice and recordkeeping requirements are not bureaucratic formalities; they are the essential “linchpin” of the Act’s enforcement scheme. Without accurate and timely information, workers cannot verify their compensation, and regulators and legal advocates cannot effectively monitor for widespread violations. Defendant’s conduct mirrors the systemic deficiencies condemned in *Stemilt*, where the failure to provide required information was found to undermine the Act’s core protective purpose. This Court should follow that precedent and hold Defendant liable for these discrete, yet interconnected, statutory violations.

Accordingly, Plaintiff respectfully requests that this Court enter judgment in its favor on the issue of liability for all claims as set forth in the Complaint. Furthermore, Plaintiff requests that the Court order the following equitable and monetary relief: (1) a permanent injunction compelling Defendant to reform its payroll, recordkeeping, and notice practices to achieve full compliance with the AWPA and its regulations; (2) an award of statutory damages for each violation as provided under 29 U.S.C. § 1853(c); (3) an order requiring Defendant to compensate Plaintiff for all reasonable attorneys’ fees, costs, and expenses incurred in this action, pursuant to 29 U.S.C. § 1854(e); and (4) any other relief the Court deems just and proper to ensure the defendant’s future compliance and to make whole the affected workers.

Only through such comprehensive relief can the Court vindicate the congressional intent behind the AWPA and deter future violations. A judgment for Plaintiff will affirm that employers of agricultural workers must adhere to the Act’s protective mandates, and that those who engage in willful patterns of noncompliance will be held fully accountable.
